name: Sara Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, and I run the ceramic tile glazing conveyor on the night shift. I'm junior on the machine; I finished secondary school and moved from boxing tiles only last year. I watch the spray pattern, pull aside tiles with a dry corner and call the setter before touching a nozzle. I like a batch whose colour matches all the way across.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband drives a delivery van, and our grown children have homes of their own. The night premium puts my operator pay above the usual rate. We have about eight months of expenses saved, and there are many other tile and packing plants nearby. I never use AI tools; I would rather ask the setter. I hope to stop at 66 in 2034, but only if written income figures show we can cover our ordinary bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my husband that no computer paints a tile corner better just because it has a fancy name. The conveyor and setter still matter. Young starters should be taught at the machine instead of being handed a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our night premium and savings put us in a good place for now. I am still learning to read the glaze, though, and I don't want a whole batch spoiled through my mistake. A quiet AI future leaves me room to learn the trade from the setter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll check the first tile of each new colour beside the setter and write down any dry corners. I'll stay on the paid night conveyor shift and add a little from each new wage payment to our savings after bills. At the family table my husband and I will keep a list of actual costs before we decide on 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the present bills. I can see a dry corner with my own eyes and ask for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you spot a dry corner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The corner goes pale before the rest of the tile dries. I put that tile aside and call the setter to check the spray head behind its guard. A bad colour run wastes more than the time it takes to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What supports the household now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband brings a regular van wage and the night premium is paid on my current rota. We have eight months saved, but we still need income after I leave. I will not call a birthday a retirement plan without the numbers.

say: **Dry tile corners** still need an operator and a setter.
New starters deserve **machine-side teaching** rather than a screen alone.
think: The **night premium** and eight-month reserve make current bills manageable.
I remain **junior at glazing** and need time to learn from the setter.
do: **Check** first tiles with the setter and record dry corners.
**Keep** earning night wages and add fresh pay to savings after bills.
feel: **Calm** about current household money with familiar tile work.
S0.quote: A bad colour run wastes more than the time it takes to stop.
fieldNote: Her **higher night pay**, regular partner wage and eight-month reserve support a calm baseline despite junior skill.
The **cost list** prepares for an income decision; new deposits come from current wages, not savings already held.

steps.text: Check first glazed tiles with setter after colour changes
Save new night-shift wages after household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software can plan tile colours before robots can pull trays from the kiln. If management changes the rota, it should tell us the paid hours plainly. I would rather the setter teach a safe nozzle check than let an AI answer tell a junior what to touch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shorter runs could take away some of my night premium. We could manage for a while with savings and my husband's van wage, but I would miss a good pay rate. Plenty of nearby plants does not mean every one has the same safe night shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll compare the posted night rota and premium with four pay slips. If there is a real cut, I'll ask the supervisor for the reason and ask my husband to help compare openings at nearby plants. If the company offers a paid guarded glaze-check place with the setter, I'll take it; I won't pay for an unproven course from our reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible loss of the night premium, though we have time and savings. A tile order on a screen does not pay my night premium.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would safe glaze-check teaching include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The setter would stop the conveyor, show me the guard and let me test spray width on a short run. The teaching needs paid hours and a real offered place. I am not going to reach past a guard after reading a machine answer online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you verify a premium cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put the four pay slips beside the next rota and look at both hours and the premium line. If either drops, I ask the supervisor about the actual amount. I will not claim a cut from a rumour in the canteen.

say: **Colour-planning software** may move before physical tile work does.
Management should provide **clear paid hours** and supervised nozzle teaching.
think: My **night premium** could shrink with shorter runs.
Our **eight-month reserve** gives time, but nearby jobs may pay less.
do: **Compare** night hours and premium with four pay slips before asking about a cut.
**Attend** setter-led glaze checking if a paid guarded place is actually offered.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic premium cut despite savings.
S1.quote: A tile order on a screen does not pay my night premium.
fieldNote: The risk is **her own night premium** through shorter runs, while robots for hands-on tile work spread later.
Her **course participation** requires an actual paid guarded place with the setter, consistent with her preference for familiar instruction.

steps.text: Compare posted night rota and premium with four pay slips
Attend glaze-check course if paid guarded setter-led place offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the family that thinking AI could sort tile orders by 2028 and capable robots might handle trays around 2031, when I am 63. That is before the 66-year stop I hope for. I would ask the plant for the rota in writing and start looking at actual openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose much of the night wage before we know if we can retire. Eight months saved and my husband's wage help, but they do not make a permanent loss painless. My main concern is finding a safe shift with enough take-home pay while I am still able to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask for a written staffing plan and a funded paid guarded tile-inspection place. If the place is offered, I'll enrol and practise with the setter. If my conveyor hours fall, I'll apply to posted safe local tile or packing jobs only where net pay after travel covers our bills; I will apply for inspection only after I qualify and only on those same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, not helpless. Nearby plants give me places to ask. A tile factory vacancy has to be real and the wage has to reach home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tile-inspection training require?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I need to identify a thin glaze patch, stop the sample conveyor and reject a bad tray. The setter should watch my hands on paid time with the guard closed. The plant should cover the course fee if it needs that qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a nearby posting worthwhile?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The post must give its base wage, hours and site. We would take off bus fare and compare the rest with household costs. I cannot take an unsafe tray shift simply because it has the word tile in the advert.

say: **2031 robots** might handle tile trays when I am 63.
I want **written staffing hours** and real nearby openings.
think: A large **night-wage loss** before 66 could delay retirement.
Our **eight-month reserve** and other plants help but cannot replace permanent income.
do: **Request** written plans and funded paid guarded inspection teaching.
**Apply** to posted safe local tile or packing work if hours fall and net pay covers bills.
feel: **Anxious** about possible major wage loss, with local options.
S2.quote: A tile factory vacancy has to be real and the wage has to reach home.
fieldNote: She sees a **large possible loss** of premium pay but has eight months saved and plentiful local jobs.
The **inspection path** needs funded paid guarded teaching and qualification; all applications need posted safe local work at viable net pay.

steps.text: Enrol in tile inspection if funded paid guarded setter-led place offered
Apply to posted safe local tile if hours fall and net pay covers bills
Apply to posted safe local packing if hours fall and net pay covers bills
Apply to posted safe local inspection if qualified, hours fall, net pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI may plan orders in 2031 and robots that handle tile trays could reach the line about 2034, when I am 66. That is the age I hope to stop. I will not tell a new starter to rely on a date before my husband and I have checked the income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If our documented post-work income covers rent and food, I can leave the conveyor at 66 before robot trays become my problem. If it does not, I may need a paid shift and a safe local fallback. The reserve is strong enough to choose carefully, not to live on forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband and I will get written figures for income after I stop and compare them with monthly costs. If the figures cover the bills, I'll leave the tile shift at 66 in 2034. If they do not and the conveyor hours fall, I'll apply to posted safe local tile roles only where net pay after travel works; I'll take funded paid guarded inspection teaching if an offered place is required for a posted inspection vacancy, then apply after qualifying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious until the income figures are in front of us. The tile conveyor might change in the same year I hope to leave it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What decides whether you leave in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We need the actual monthly income available after my wage ends, not a guess about any payment. We will set it beside rent, food and transport. If it does not cover them, I keep working while a safe paid shift is available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would an inspection job differ?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A tile posting needs a safe guard, a workable shift and enough net pay after travel. An inspection post also needs an actual funded paid guarded place and a practical pass. I will not spend our reserve on a certificate that does not lead to a real opening.

say: **2031 planning AI** gives a few years before tile-handling robots around 2034.
Leaving at **66** depends on written income covering household costs.
think: The **eight-month reserve** cannot fund an unlimited retirement.
If the figures fail, I may need **paid tile work** when robots arrive.
do: **Compare** documented post-work income and stop tile work in 2034 only if bills are covered.
**Apply** to safe posted local tile or qualified inspection jobs if still working, hours fall and net pay works.
feel: **Anxious** until actual retirement income is checked.
S3.quote: The tile conveyor might change in the same year I hope to leave it.
fieldNote: Her **2034 exit** is a real conditional decision, not merely an enquiry or an assumed entitlement.
If still employed, the **inspection fallback** requires funded paid guarded teaching, qualification, a posted safe local role and sufficient net pay.

steps.text: Stop tile shift at 66 in 2034 if documented income covers bills
Attend inspection if offered funded paid guarded place for posted vacancy
Apply to posted safe local tile if still working, hours fall, net pay sufficient
Apply to posted safe local inspection if qualified, still working, hours fall, net pay sufficient

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children that thinking AI might organise tile orders in 2036, when I am 68, and capable robots could handle trays about 2039, when I am 71. I hope to have finished paid shifts by then. I will not call a future payment certain until we see it in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have eight months saved and a good current wage, but those are not lifetime income. If the verified figures let me stop at 66 in 2034, I will. If they fall short, I may still be on a conveyor when AI reaches order planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year my husband and I will compare documented post-work income with our rent, food and other bills. I'll keep the night shift while the figures are checked. If income covers costs, I'll stop in 2034 at 66; if I am still employed after 2036 and hours fall, I'll apply to posted safe local tile work only when net pay after travel covers the household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about an unknown income figure, though the time and savings give us choices. A date on the tile factory calendar will not pay our food bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which figures would support stopping in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would use actual income that will be available after my wage stops, and list the bills we still have. We cannot invent a pension or assume the delivery van will run every day. If the total is short, I keep a paid job while I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would a later tile application happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look for a real tile posting with guards, paid hours and a base wage that still works after bus fare. I would apply only if I were still working and my shifts had fallen. If I have already left with enough income, no job search is needed.

say: **2036 AI** and later robots leave time to verify income.
I will **leave in 2034** only if our bills are covered.
think: Eight months saved is **not lifetime income** after work.
If documented income is short, I could be **working after 2036**.
do: **Check** actual post-work income against bills and stop at 66 only if affordable.
**Keep** earning until then; apply after 2036 only if still employed, hours fall and a safe local job pays enough.
feel: **Uneasy** while retirement income remains unverified, with time to plan.
S4.quote: A date on the tile factory calendar will not pay our food bill.
fieldNote: The **2034 stop branch** follows a written income comparison and is not an assumed benefit or automatic retirement.
The **later application** requires continued employment, lost hours and an actual safe local tile post with adequate net pay.

steps.text: Compare documented post-work income with household bills
Keep paid tile night shift while income figures are checked
Stop tile shift at 66 in 2034 if documented income covers bills
Apply to posted safe local tile if employed after 2036, hours fall, net pay sufficient

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case. A robot line could take my night wage at 63, before we know whether 66 is affordable. Written staffing hours, funded paid guarded tile inspection and real safe local posts with enough pay after travel would help. My husband and I will check post-work income before any notice to leave.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who looks at the first tile after a nozzle change. A pale corner can travel through a whole batch before the glaze is dry.

headlineQuote: A pale corner can travel through a whole batch before the glaze is dry.
portrait: **Sara**, 58, is a junior tile-glazing operator with secondary schooling who never uses AI tools.
She and her van-driver husband have **grown children**, higher night pay, eight months saved and many nearby plants.
Her **traditional outlook** values work, family and setter-led teaching; she wants a real wage and a safe guarded machine.
She is **anxious** about a fast night-wage loss; stopping at 66 depends on documented household income covering costs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring tile-handling robots by 2031, cutting night pay at 63 before retirement is affordable.
whatWouldHelp: **Written staffing hours**, funded paid guarded inspection and real safe local work at bill-covering net pay would help.
